{{Short description|Relative distance of a point from a circle}}
[[File:Potenz-geom-e.svg|thumb|upright=0.8|Geometric meaning]]

In elementary plane [[geometry]], the '''power of a point''' is a [[real number]] that reflects the relative [[distance (mathematics)|distance]] of a given [[point (geometry)|point]] from a given [[circle]]. It was introduced by [[Jakob Steiner]] in 1826.<ref>Jakob Steiner: ''Einige geometrische Betrachtungen'', 1826, S. 164</ref>

Specifically, the power <math>\Pi(P)</math> of a point <math>P</math> with respect to a circle <math>c</math> with center <math>O</math> and radius <math>r</math> is defined by
: <math>\Pi(P)=|PO|^2 - r^2.</math>
If <math>P</math> is ''outside'' the circle, then <math>\Pi(P)>0</math>,<br>
if <math>P</math> is ''on'' the circle, then <math>\Pi(P)=0</math> and <br>
if <math>P</math> is ''inside'' the circle, then <math>\Pi(P)<0</math>.

Due to the [[Pythagorean theorem]] the number <math>\Pi(P)</math> has the simple geometric meanings shown in the diagram: For a point <math>P</math> outside the circle, <math>\Pi(P)</math> is the squared ''tangential distance'' <math>|PT|</math> of point <math>P</math> to a point <math>T</math> on the circle <math>c</math>.

Points with equal power, [[isolines]] of <math>\Pi(P)</math>, are circles [[concentric]] to the original circle <math>c</math>.

Steiner used the power of a point for proofs of several statements on circles, for example:
* Determination of a circle, that intersects four circles by the same angle.<ref>Steiner, p. 163</ref>
* Solving the [[problem of Apollonius]]
* Construction of the [[Malfatti circles]]:<ref>Steiner, p. 178</ref> For a given triangle determine three circles, which touch each other and two sides of the triangle each.
* [[Spherical trigonometry|Spherical]] version of Malfatti's problem:<ref>Steiner, p. 182</ref> The triangle is a spherical one.

Essential tools for investigations on circles are the [[radical axis]] of two circles and the [[Power center (geometry)|radical center]] of three circles.

The [[power diagram]] of a set of circles divides the plane into regions within which the circle minimizing the power is constant.

More generally, French mathematician  [[Edmond Laguerre]] defined the power of a point with respect to any [[algebraic curve]] in a similar way.

== Geometric properties ==
Besides the properties mentioned in the lead there are further properties:

=== Orthogonal circle ===
[[File:Potenz-okreis-e.svg|thumb|upright=1.1|Orthogonal circle (green)]]
For any point <math>P</math> ''outside'' of the circle <math>c</math> there are two tangent points  <math>T_1,T_2</math> on circle <math>c</math>, which have equal distance to <math>P</math>. Hence the circle <math>o</math> with center <math>P</math> through <math>T_1</math> passes <math>T_2</math>, too, and intersects <math>c</math> orthogonal:
* The circle with center <math>P</math> and radius <math>\sqrt{\Pi(P)}</math> intersects circle <math>c</math> ''orthogonal''.
[[File:Potenz-schnittw-kreis-e.svg|thumb|upright=1.15|Angle between two circles]]

If the radius <math>\rho</math> of the circle centered at <math>P</math> is different from <math>\sqrt{\Pi(P)}</math> one gets the angle of intersection <math>\varphi</math> between the two circles applying the [[Law of cosines]] (see the diagram):
:<math>\rho^2+r^2-2\rho r \cos\varphi=|PO|^2 </math>
:<math> \rightarrow \ 
\cos\varphi=\frac{\rho^2+r^2-|PO|^2}{2\rho r}=\frac{\rho^2-\Pi(P)}{2\rho r}</math>
(<math>PS_1</math> and <math>OS_1</math> are [[Normal (geometry)|normal]]s to the circle tangents.)

If <math>P</math> lies inside the blue circle, then <math>\Pi(P)<0</math> and <math> \varphi</math> is always different from <math>90^\circ</math>.
 
If the angle <math>\varphi</math> is given, then one gets the radius <math>\rho</math> by solving the [[quadratic equation]]
:<math>\rho^2-2\rho r \cos\varphi-\Pi(P)=0</math>.

=== Intersecting secants theorem, intersecting chords theorem ===
[[File:Potenz-sek-sehne-e.svg|thumb|upright=0.8|Secant-, chord-theorem]]
For the ''[[intersecting secants theorem]]'' and [[intersecting chords theorem|''chord theorem'']] the power of a point plays the role of an [[Invariant (mathematics)|invariant]]:

* ''Intersecting secants theorem'': For a point <math>P</math> ''outside'' a circle <math>c</math> and the intersection points <math>S_1,S_2</math> of a [[secant line]] <math> g</math> with <math>c</math> the following statement is true: <math>|PS_1| \cdot |PS_2|= \Pi(P)</math>, hence the product is independent of line <math>g</math>. If <math>g</math> is tangent then <math>S_1=S_2</math> and the statement is the ''[[tangent-secant theorem]]''.
* ''[[Intersecting chords theorem]]'': For a point <math>P</math> ''inside'' a circle <math>c</math> and the intersection points <math>S_1,S_2</math> of a secant line <math> g</math> with <math>c</math> the following statement is true: <math>|PS_1| \cdot |PS_2|= -\Pi(P)</math>, hence the product is independent of line <math>g</math>.

=== Radical axis ===
Let <math>P</math> be a point and <math>c_1,c_2</math> two non concentric circles with 
centers <math>O_1,O_2</math> and radii <math>r_1,r_2</math>. Point <math>P</math> has the power <math>\Pi_i(P)</math> with respect to circle <math>c_i</math>. The set of all points <math>P</math> with <math>\Pi_1(P)=\Pi_2(P)</math> is a line called ''[[radical axis]]''. It contains possible common points of the circles and is perpendicular to line <math>\overline{O_1O_2}</math>.

== Secants theorem, chords theorem: common proof ==
[[File:Potenz-sek-sehne-beweis-e.svg|thumb|upright=0.8|Secant-/chord-theorem: proof]]
Both theorems, including the ''tangent-secant theorem'', can be proven uniformly:

Let <math>P:\vec p</math> be a point, <math>c: \vec x^2-r^2=0</math> a circle with the origin as its center and <math>\vec v</math> an arbitrary [[unit vector]]. The parameters  <math>t_1,t_2</math> of possible common points of line  <math>g: \vec x=\vec p+t\vec v</math> (through <math>P</math>) and circle <math>c</math> can be determined by inserting the [[parametric equation]] into the circle's equation:
:<math>(\vec p+t\vec v)^2-r^2=0 \quad  \rightarrow \quad
t^2+2t\;\vec p\cdot\vec v +\vec p^2-r^2=0 \ . </math>
From [[Vieta's theorem]] one finds:
:<math>t_1\cdot t_2=\vec p^2-r^2 =\Pi(P)</math>. (independent of <math>\vec v</math>)
<math>\Pi(P)</math> is the power of <math>P</math> with respect to circle <math>c</math>.

Because of <math>|\vec v|=1</math> one gets the following statement for the points <math>S_1,S_2</math>:
:<math>|PS_1|\cdot|PS_2|=t_1t_2=\Pi(P)\ </math>, if <math>P</math> is outside the circle,
:<math>|PS_1|\cdot|PS_2|=-t_1t_2=-\Pi(P)\ </math>, if <math>P</math> is inside the circle (<math>t_1,t_2</math> have different signs !).

In case of <math>t_1=t_2</math> line <math>g</math> is a tangent  and <math>\Pi(P)</math> the square of the tangential distance of point <math>P</math> to circle <math>c</math>.

== Similarity points, common power of two circles ==
=== Similarity points ===
Similarity points are an essential tool for Steiner's investigations on circles.<ref>Steiner: p. 170,171</ref>

Given two circles
:<math>\ c_1: (\vec x -\vec m_1)^2-r_1^2=0, \quad  c_2: (\vec x -\vec m_2)^2-r_2^2=0 \ .</math>
A [[homothety]] ([[Similarity (geometry)|similarity]]) <math>\sigma</math>, that maps <math>c_1</math> onto <math>c_2</math> stretches (jolts) radius <math> r_1</math> to <math>r_2</math> and has its center <math>Z:\vec z</math> on the line <math>\overline{M_1 M_2}</math>, because <math>\sigma(M_1)=M_2</math>. If center <math>Z</math> is between <math>M_1,M_2</math> the scale factor is <math>s=-\tfrac{r_2}{r_1}</math>. In the other case <math>s=\tfrac{r_2}{r_1}</math>. In any case:
:<math>\sigma(\vec m_1)=\vec z + s(\vec m_1-\vec z)=\vec m_2</math>.
Inserting <math>s=\pm\tfrac{r_2}{r_1}</math> and solving for <math>\vec z</math> yields:
:<math> \vec z= \frac{r_1\vec m_2\mp r_2\vec m_1}{r_1\mp r_2}</math>.
[[File:Kreise2-aehnlpunkte-var.svg|thumb|upright=2|Similarity points of two circles: various cases]]
Point <math display="block">E:\vec e=\frac{r_1\vec m_2-r_2\vec m_1}{r_1-r_2}</math> is called the ''exterior similarity point'' and <math display="block">I:\vec i=\frac{r_1\vec m_2+r_2\vec m_1}{r_1+r_2}</math> is called the ''inner similarity point''.

In case of <math>M_1=M_2</math> one gets <math>E=I=M_i</math>.<br>
In case of <math>r_1=r_2</math>: <math>E</math> is the [[point at infinity]] of line <math>\overline{M_1 M_2}</math> and <math>I</math> is the center of <math>M_1,M_2</math>.<br>
In case of <math>r_1=|EM_1|</math> the circles touch each other at point <math>E</math> ''inside'' (both circles on the same side of the common tangent line).<br>
In case of <math>r_1=|IM_1|</math> the circles touch each other at point <math>I</math> ''outside'' (both circles on different sides of the common tangent line).

Further more:
* If the circles lie ''disjoint'' (the discs have no points in common), the outside common tangents meet at <math>E</math> and the inner ones at <math>I</math>.
* If one circle is contained ''within the other'', the points <math>E,I</math> lie  ''within'' both circles.
* The pairs <math>M_1,M_2;E,I</math> are [[projective harmonic conjugate]]: Their [[cross ratio]] is <math>(M_1,M_2;E,I)=-1</math>.

[[Monge's theorem]] states: The ''outer'' similarity points of three disjoint circles lie on a line.

=== Common power of two circles ===
[[File:Kreis-2-aehnlpunkte.svg|thumb|upright=1.6|Similarity points of two circles and their common power]]

Let <math>c_1,c_2</math> be two circles, <math>E</math> their outer similarity point and <math>g</math> a line through <math>E</math>, which meets the two circles at four points <math>G_1,H_1,G_2,H_2</math>. From the defining property of point <math>E</math> one gets 
:<math>\frac{|EG_1|}{|EG_2|}=\frac{r_1}{r_2}=\frac{|EH_1|}{|EH_2|}\ </math>
:<math> \rightarrow \ |EG_1|\cdot|EH_2|=|EH_1|\cdot|EG_2|\ </math>
and from the secant theorem (see above) the two equations 
:<math>|EG_1|\cdot|EH_1|=\Pi_1(E),\quad |EG_2|\cdot|EH_2|=\Pi_2(E) .</math>
Combining these three equations yields:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\Pi_1(E)\cdot\Pi_2(E) &=|EG_1|\cdot|EH_1|\cdot|EG_2|\cdot|EH_2| \\
&=|EG_1|^2\cdot|EH_2|^2= |EG_2|^2\cdot|EH_1|^2 \ .
\end{align}</math>
Hence: <math display="block">|EG_1|\cdot|EH_2|= |EG_2| \cdot |EH_1|=\sqrt{ \Pi_1(E)\cdot\Pi_2(E)} </math> (independent of line <math>g</math> !).
The analog statement for the inner similarity point <math>I</math> is true, too.

The invariants <math display="inline">\sqrt{\Pi_1(E)\cdot\Pi_2(E)},\ \sqrt{ \Pi_1(I)\cdot\Pi_2(I)} </math> are called by Steiner ''common power of the two circles'' (''gemeinschaftliche Potenz der beiden Kreise bezüglich ihrer Ähnlichkeitspunkte'').<ref>Steiner: p. 175</ref>

The pairs <math>G_1,H_2</math> and <math>H_1,G_2</math> of points are ''antihomologous'' points. The pairs <math>G_1,G_2</math> and <math>H_1,H_2</math> are ''homologous''.<ref>Michel Chasles, C. H. Schnuse: ''Die Grundlehren der neuern Geometrie, erster Theil'', Verlag Leibrock, Braunschweig, 1856, p. 312</ref><ref> William J. M'Clelland: ''A Treatise on the Geometry of the Circle and Some Extensions to Conic Sections by the Method of Reciprocation'',1891, Verlag:  Creative Media Partners, LLC, {{ISBN|978-0-344-90374-8}}, p. 121,220</ref>

=== Determination of a circle that is tangent to two circles ===
[[File:Kreise2-ap-2sek.svg|thumb|upright=1.6|Common power of two circles: application]]
[[File:Kreise2-ap-beruehrk.svg|thumb|upright=1.6|Circles tangent to two circles]]
For a second secant through  <math>E</math>:
:<math>|EH_1|\cdot|EG_2|= |EH'_1|\cdot|EG'_2|</math>
From the secant theorem one gets:
:The four points <math>H_1,G_2,H'_1,G'_2</math> lie on a circle.
And analogously:
: The four points <math>G_1,H_2,G'_1,H'_2</math> lie on a circle, too.
Because the radical lines of three circles meet at the radical (see: article radical line), one gets:
:The secants <math>\overline{H_1H'_1},\;\overline{G_2G'_2}</math> meet on the radical axis of the given two circles. 

Moving the lower secant (see diagram) towards the upper one, the red circle becomes a circle, that is tangent to both given circles. The center of the tangent circle is the intercept of the lines <math>\overline{M_1H_1},\overline{M_2G_2}</math>. The secants <math>\overline{H_1H'_1}, \overline{G_2G'_2}</math> become tangents at the points <math>H_1,G_2</math>. The tangents intercept at the radical line <math>p</math> (in the diagram yellow).

Similar considerations generate the second tangent circle, that meets the given circles at the points <math>G_1,H_2</math> (see diagram).

All [[tangent circles]] to the given circles can be found by varying line <math>g</math>.

;Positions of the centers

[[File:Kreise2-ap-beruehrkreise-n.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|Circles tangent to two circles]]
If <math>X </math> is the center and <math>\rho</math> the radius of the circle, that is tangent to the given circles at the points <math>H_1,G_2</math>, then:
:<math>\rho=|XM_1|-r_1=|XM_2|-r_2 </math>
:<math> \rightarrow \ |XM_2|-|XM_1|=r_2-r_1 . </math>

Hence: the centers lie on a [[hyperbola]] with
:foci <math>M_1,M_2</math>, 
:distance of the vertices{{clarify|date=June 2022}} <math>2a=r_2-r_1</math>, 
:center <math>M</math> is the center of  <math>M_1,M_2</math> ,
:linear eccentricity <math>c=\tfrac{|M_1M_2|}{2}</math> and 
:<math>\ b^2=e^2-a^2=\tfrac{|M_1M_2|^2-(r_2-r_1)^2}{4}</math>{{clarify|date=June 2022}}.  

Considerations on the outside tangent circles lead to the analog result: 

If <math>X </math> is the center and <math>\rho</math> the radius of the circle, that is tangent to the given circles at the points <math>G_1,H_2</math>, then:
:<math>\rho=|XM_1|+r_1=|XM_2|+r_2 </math>
:<math> \rightarrow \ |XM_2|-|XM_1|=-(r_2-r_1) . </math>

The centers lie on the same hyperbola, but on the right branch.

See also [[Problem of Apollonius#Solution methods|Problem of Apollonius]].

[[File:Potenz-kugel-sek-e.svg|thumb|Power of a point with respect to a sphere]]

== Power with respect to a sphere ==
The idea of the power of a point with respect to a circle can be extended to a sphere.<ref>K.P. Grothemeyer: ''Analytische Geometrie'', Sammlung Göschen 65/65A, Berlin 1962, S. 54</ref> The secants and chords theorems are true for a sphere, too, and can be proven literally as in the circle case.

==Darboux product==
The power of a point is a special case of the Darboux product between two circles, which is given by<ref>Pierre Larochelle, J. Michael McCarthy:''Proceedings of the 2020 USCToMM Symposium on Mechanical Systems and Robotics'', 2020, Springer-Verlag, {{ISBN|978-3-030-43929-3}}, p. 97</ref>
:<math>\left| A_1A_2 \right|^2-r_1^2-r_2^2 \, </math>
where ''A''<sub>1</sub> and ''A''<sub>2</sub> are the centers of the two circles and ''r''<sub>1</sub> and ''r''<sub>2</sub> are their radii. The power of a point arises in the special case that one of the radii is zero.

If the two circles are orthogonal, the Darboux product vanishes.

If the two circles intersect, then their Darboux product is

:<math>2r_1 r_2 \cos\varphi \, </math>
where ''&phi;'' is the angle of intersection (see section ''orthogonal circle'').

==Laguerre's theorem==
[[Edmond Laguerre|Laguerre]] defined the power of a point ''P'' with respect to an algebraic curve of degree ''n'' to be the sum of the distances from the point to the intersections of a circle through the point with the curve, divided by the ''n''th power of the diameter ''d''. Laguerre showed that this number is independent of the diameter {{harv|Laguerre|1905}}. In the case when the algebraic curve is a circle this is not quite the same as the power of a point with respect to a circle defined in the rest of this article, but differs from it by a factor of ''d''<sup>2</sup>.
